newsitem.title: UK: Benign UK producer prices bode well for lower RPI.
newsitem.headline: Benign UK producer prices bode well for lower RPI.

text.p: A sharp fall in input prices in June and a surprise fall in factory gate prices bodes well for lower high street price inflation later this year, and perhaps fewer rate rises than some economists fear.

"This bodes very well for retail price inflation falling and remaining low this year and is good news for the interest rate profile too. We see rates peaking at 7.5 percent next year," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Output prices fell by 0.2 percent in June for year-on-year growth of 1.1 percent compared with 1.0 percent in May.
Input prices fell by 0.8 percent on a seasonally-adjusted basis. Year-on-year input prices were down 8.6 percent.
The drop in output prices shows firms are passing on lower costs to their customers. David said with consumers still highly sensitive to high street prices, shops will have to do the same.
"The signs we are seeing suggest consumers are still very sensitive to prices and lower costs mean that shops can expand their margins without raising their prices."
Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS, agreed the outlook for retail prices is very promising.

"Inflation in (the manufacturing) sector is practically non-existent and with sterling continuing to strengthen there is every prospect that this will remain the case for some time. As such the prospects for retail price inflation remain excellent."
He said output and retail prices generally move in tandem, with the average difference between their respective inflation rates being just 0.5 percent over the past 10 years.
The pound's upward march began the week with renewed vigour and reached fresh highs above the 3.0 mark level. Sterling has gained around 24 percent on a trade-weighed basis since last August.
While this has caused problems for manufacturers trying to sell their goods abroad, falling input costs mean margins should not have been damaged, economists said.

"Lower input prices will help mitigate some of the trouble the exchange rate is causing for manufacturers. Their margins are probably still growing because of these low costs," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
